---
title: "Evolution of Application Architecture"
description: "A worked lesson in the shop-service microservices learning path."
---

**Source:** Supplied Spring Cloud course, Day 1 §1.1. **Example:** the shop system with Product, Order and User services.

## Start with the shop, not a framework

A small online shop offers three business operations: look up a product, identify a customer and place an order. The first implementation may contain three modules in **one process**. A customer placing an order invokes the Product and User modules as ordinary function calls. All three modules are deployed together.

As the shop grows, teams may want to release the Product catalogue independently of Order processing. This is an organisational and operational requirement, not something a large number of Java classes automatically creates.

## Four architectural stages

**Monolith:** one deployment contains the product, order and user logic. It can still be internally modular. Calls are local, transactions are easier, and debugging is straightforward. A change to the Product module generally triggers a deployment of the whole application.

**Vertically separated applications:** independent business applications are deployed apart. The shop's catalogue and checkout could become separate deployables even if each remains a monolith. The boundary may still be too coarse for more teams or workload differences.

**Service-oriented architecture (SOA):** applications share service contracts and reusable capabilities. The provided course introduces SOA in terms of service composition and, in some historical deployments, an enterprise service bus. An ESB is **not a required property** of all SOA systems.

**Microservices:** smaller, business-aligned services can be deployed and scaled independently. The shop may run several Product instances while deploying Order separately. Calls now cross a network boundary, and ownership of data becomes an explicit design decision.

## Compare the coupling

~~~text
Monolith:   Checkout -> Product module (same process)
Separated:  Order service --HTTP--> Product service
~~~

A service boundary adds deployment independence but also timeouts, failures, authentication, tracing and cross-service data consistency. Merely distributing the code can make a small system worse.

## When not to split

If a tiny team maintains one low-traffic shop, start with a modular monolith. Move to separate services when independent release cadence, team ownership, isolation or scalability can justify the operational cost.

## Review and extension

Explain this design to another engineer using the running example. Identify one benefit, one failure mode and the condition under which you would choose a simpler design.

**Try it:** The [shop lab](../examples/README.md) uses several HTTP servers in a single process to teach boundaries; it does not claim to implement isolated production deployments.

## Mathematical Abstraction

A split moves a module call across a process boundary.

$$
\operatorname{Cost}_{\rm remote}=\operatorname{Cost}_{\rm local}+L_{\rm network}+L_{\rm serialise}+L_{\rm protocol}
$$

This is an illustrative cost decomposition; the addends depend on what is counted and need measurement. Deployment independence may justify the overhead.
